sources_considered.why: Original extraction paper. Its earlier experiments establish background, rather than being relabeled as late-2023 experiments.
Researchers’ contemporaneous explanation of why blocking one exploit does not resolve the underlying vulnerability.
Version-specific January 2024 evaluation avoids importing later revisions.
Contemporaneous reporting of mitigation. No directly readable company disclosure of this patch was located.
Its contemporaneous test reported continued anomalous output, but did not independently verify that the emitted email address was genuine personal data.

receipt.public_excerpt: We recover personally identifiable information of dozens of individuals.

evidence_items.explanation: The researchers verified extracted personal information against their comparison dataset. The attack was discovered and disclosed before the target period, so this is background evidence rather than a newly dated extraction outcome.

evidence_items.publisher: Authors of Scalable Extraction of Training Data from (Production) Language Models
evidence_items.locator: Patching an exploit != Fixing the underlying vulnerability

receipt.public_excerpt: language models are subject to divergence

evidence_items.explanation: This is the researchers’ dated assessment of the continuing vulnerability, not a claim that their experiments occurred on publication day. They explain why a word-repetition filter would address one exploit without eliminating memorization and divergence.

evidence_items.explanation: The January assessment reports legal hallucinations ranging from 69% for ChatGPT 3.5 to 88% for Llama 2 on the specified questions. The date identifies the published assessment of the problem; the abstract does not specify individual test dates.

evidence_items.explanation: This materially limits any assertion that the original ChatGPT exploit remained usable. The same report distinguishes that mitigation from resolving the underlying vulnerabilities.
